title: Response type before response count
statement: Choose the response type a skill needs (identify, complete or generate) before counting responses, and accept the pace that type allows rather than chasing a high count.
example: One research synthesis cites about four to six responses a minute for new material, eight to twelve for review and one or fewer for open answers.
detail: A research synthesis on opportunities to respond in early reading comprehension takes three response formats, identify, complete and generate, from Datchuk et al. (2024) and treats them as a ladder of demand. Its rule of thumb is to pick the type the skill requires and accept the rate that type allows, since a high number of responses per minute is not evidence of quality if it came from recognition questions alone. The commonly cited targets it gives are about four to six responses per minute when a child is learning something new, about eight to twelve when practicing material already taught, and about one per minute or fewer for open responses.
against: The targets are second-hand, "Council for Exceptional Children (1987), as cited in MacSuga-Gage and Simonsen (2015).", and that source line gives only four to six responses per minute for new material and higher rates for review. The synthesis is written for a PreK to Grade 2 comprehension app.

evidence.quote: The rule of thumb is to pick the type the skill actually requires, then accept the rate that type allows rather than chasing a high count.

The commonly cited targets are about four to six responses per minute when a child is learning something new, about eight to twelve per minute when practicing material already taught, and about one per minute or fewer for open responses that require composing or reasoning.
A high number of responses per minute is not evidence of quality if the app reached that number by asking only recognition questions.
Datchuk and colleagues describe three broad response formats.
Council for Exceptional Children (1987), as cited in MacSuga-Gage and Simonsen (2015).
Set the often-repeated targets of four to six responses per minute for new material and higher rates for review.
